extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, instrument-makers, astronomers, miners, and Royal Society readers (17th-century scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reports on constructing hygroscopic recording devices, making and interpreting observational records (astronomical occultations, natural-history observations), and practical detection methods for minerals; aimed at practitioners and readers of the Philosophical Transactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of the first contrivance (Figure A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A AAA is the frame of wood, for the two pannels of deal to play loose in, at top and bottom, to which at the two ends they are fastened. — BB, the two pannels of slit deal, three feet deep, and three feet broad a-piece, with a distance left in the middle for the scope of the motion. — C, the hand fastened by the axletree to the plate, and also with nail-holes which are to fasten it to the middle of the pannel, within half an inch of the scope for motion; at the lower or shorter end of the axletree there is fastened, by a wire like an S, a small silver chain within a straw's breadth of the axletree; which chain is to be carried and placed across the distance between the two pannels, and fastened to the opposite pannel by a brass noose, through which it is to slip, so as to be taken up or let down at pleasure. — D, the roller, with a weight annexed, which by a string is fastened to the lower end of the hand C; so that, as it relaxes and gives way, the weight will adjust the motion of the hand to the index E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include frame and panel dimensions (panels ~3 ft x 3 ft), provide axletree-mounted hand, use small silver chain and brass noose with adjustable links to alter play; attach roller with weight via string to control hand motion; paste a paper index opposite the hand; plan for adjustability so the chain can be taken up or let down to change motion range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment of chain placement and effect on motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Now if the chain be placed near the axis, the motion will be the nicer and larger; if farther off then it will be less: For instance, the motion of 2 more than that of 3, and 3 than that of 4, &c. as may be seen by the figures 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; which are placed in this figure below the hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position the chain nearer the rotational axis to amplify and refine motion; move it outward to reduce amplitude. Provide illustrative figures and allow experimental adjustment to achieve desired sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using the device as a weather and seasonal indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: These pannels of deal board move by shrinking most in summer, and swelling most in winter seasons; ... For the most part, especially in spring and summer, this motion happens only in the day time; ... The winds being in the north, north-east and east, winter and summer, for the most part at that time the deal shrinks in the night as well as in the day; ... on the contrary, the south winds blowing, or the west and south-west, the deal then always relaxes, or at least is at a stand, provided this happen in the day time. — By a constant observation of this experiment of the deal's motion and rest, you may be able to guess at the situation of the wind, without a weather-cock, provided you have a common and a sealed thermometer. Also you may know the time of the year; for, in the spring it moves quicker and more, than in winter; in summer it shrinks more than in the spring; in autumn it is less in motion than in summer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record panel motion over time alongside temperature (sealed thermometer). Use daily patterns and wind-direction correlations (north/northeast/east → shrinking; south/south-west → relaxing) to infer wind situation and season. Collect constant observations to build reliable correlations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sizing pulleys and gearing for circular (annual) recorder
rubrics_metrics.description: The circumference of the smaller pulley or roller Bb, on which the chain is fastened, is to be no larger than just so much scope or distance as the two pannels make by the extremity of their utmost swelling or shrinking; and so one full revolution of the hand on the index may answer the greatest shrinking and swelling in the year, and the distance between the two rollers or pulleys fixed on the axis must be the thickness of the pannels; so that the weight is to play or move on the one side of the pannel, and the chain on the other, without disturbance or rubbing against the sides of the pannel or the cross, between which, in the middle they are to be placed out of sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the smaller pulley's circumference to match the total expected seasonal panel displacement so one revolution = annual range. Set pulley spacing equal to panel thickness to avoid rubbing; arrange weights and chains oppositely so motion is smooth and concealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material selection and seasoning test for deal board
rubrics_metrics.description: The deal board should be of the finest and straightest grained dram deal laid to dry two or three years. And to know whether it be sufficiently seasoned, take a small part of it, and weigh it in a nice pair of scales, and if you find the weight not increased many grains in wet weather, nor decreased in dry, you may then conclude it fit for your purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-seasoned, straight-grained deal dried 2–3 years. Test seasoning by weighing a sample across wet/dry conditions: acceptable if weight changes only by a few grains; otherwise continue seasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording occultation observations and correcting clock error
rubrics_metrics.description: By several altitudes of the sun's lower limb, taken before the occultation, it was found that the error of the clock was 4m. 55 s. too slow. Then, afternoon, the sky being very clear, the following observations were taken: [detailed time-by-clock, distances, altitudes, and remarks]. Having carefully considered the moon's parallaxes, in the observations of this occultation ... I find from the immersion the difference of meridians between Greenwich and Oxford 4m. 57s.; between Greenwich and Dantzic, 1 h. 14m. 50s. Also by the emersion the first of those differences is found 4 m. 59s.; and the latter 1 h. 14m. 41s. Which near agreement shows the exactness of all the observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before event, measure solar altitudes to estimate clock error. Record times, names of reference stars, altitudes, and angular distances carefully. Use immersion/emersion timings from multiple sites to compute meridian differences and validate observational exactness by agreement between independent measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracing planetary occultation using telescopic lunar features
rubrics_metrics.description: If it be asked how I could thus exactly trace out the planet's passage behind the moon, and even that of her obscure part; it proceeded from hence, that by those tubes of mine I could very distinctly perceive the principal of the larger spots in the shaded part of the moon; so that I could observe very plainly, that Mars emerged near the middle of Palus Maeotis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use telescopes to identify and register prominent lunar surface features (spots, mounts, paludes) in the shaded portion; reference those landmarks when timing immersion/emersion to determine the planet's path behind the lunar disc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating claims of petrifaction vs vegetative origin of figured stones
rubrics_metrics.description: I cannot say, that my own observations have ever yet presented me with an ocular evidence of the thing: I only find, that the thing supposed to be petrified, becomes first crusted over with a stony concretion, and afterwards, as that rots away inwardly, the lapidescent juice insinuates itself by degrees into its room, and makes at last a firm stone, resembling the thing in shape; which may lead some to believe it really petrified. But though a real petrifaction were allowed in some cases, it would not be rational to plead this in all the figured stones we see, on account of the many grounds we have for the contrary. ... let them descend into coal mines, where generally with us the clifts near the coal are all wrought with curious representations of several sorts of herbs ... and though it could, here can be no colour for a petrifaction, it being only a superficial delineation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume petrifaction without ocular/experimental evidence. Distinguish superficial mineral delineation (e.g., coal-clift fern-like patterns, snow figura­tions) from true internal petrifaction; consider alternative mechanisms (crusting, lapidescent infiltration, seminal 'root' or formative causes). Seek direct, repeatable observation before asserting petrifaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improving miner detection of ore via smell and baroscopic pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a constant opinion among our miners, that lead ore discovers itself by an oily smell, and that chiefly in a morning, a little before the rising of the sun, especially when some showers have fallen in the night: this being so, I find two things in the Transactions, which give me hopes that this way of discovery may be much improved by art: the first is an intimation of a way shown by Sir William Petty, in his tract of double proportions, whereby we may discover a smell at a great distance, and so consequently the intenseness and remissness of it near at hand, wherein the chief difficulty will consist; ... The second thing is the statical baroscope of Mr. Boyle, which I conceive may give us some light of their true source, there being probably at that place a considerable variation in the pressure of the atmosphere by reason of the mineral-steams which are there in the greatest abundance. I am not ignorant that some strongly fermented beds ... send forth a ranker smell than ore itself, which may now and then deceive us; but because for the most part these are concomitants of ore, we may not look upon the attempt as fruitless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine methods: remote smell-detection (per Petty's 'double proportions' idea) to detect and localize odours, and use sensitive baroscopic instruments (Boyle's statical baroscope) to detect local atmospheric pressure variations due to mineral-steams. Be aware of false positives from fermented mineral beds and interpret smells in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for assessing mathematical and geometrical treatises (book review standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: This author, in his first proposition, demonstrates all the proportions of the lines, which coming from one point, or being parallel among themselves, and meeting the sections, are cut by these sections, or by the lines that join the contacts ... which seems to him very easy to understand, forasmuch as it is nothing else but a continual repetition of the application of one only line cut in three parts, which line he calls cut harmonically; not that the parts taken separately are in harmonical proportion, but that, by taking one of the extremes for one, and the same with that of the middle for another, and the whole for the last, these three lines should be in harmonical proportion. ... He has also given a method of demonstrating the sections of the conic surfaces that have for base parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas; as also those of cylindrical surfaces, which have for base the same curves as well as the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate clarity of propositions, comprehensiveness (coverage of classical results e.g., Apollonius), novelty of methods or proofs, practical usefulness of additional propositions, and whether demonstrations simplify or extend classical material. Note pedagogical clarity and applicability to measurement/surveying tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying corrupted rye and diagnosing associated health effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The rye in Sologne ... sometimes so corrupted, that those who did eat of the bread which had much of this corrupted grain in it, were seized with a gangrene; ... These grains of rye are black without, and pretty white within, and when they are dry, they are harder and closer than the natural good grain. They have no ill taste. Some of them had hanging at their basis a substance of a honey-taste and consistence. They become much longer in the ear than the other, some of them being 13 or 14 lines long, and 2 lines broad, and at times seven or eight of them are found in one ear. ... The effects are, to dry up the milk in women; to cause sometimes malignant fevers accompanied with drowsiness and raving; to breed the gangrene in the arms but mostly in the legs, which it first seizes, as the scurvy does. The only remedy for this gangrene is to cut off the part affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose corrupted rye by grain morphology (black exterior, white interior, harder when dry, honey-tasting substance at base, unusually long grains, multiple grains per ear). Correlate consumption history with symptoms (numbness, painless gangrene, drying of milk, fevers). Recognize lack of specific remedy beyond excision/amputation; consider preventive treatments (hot spirits, volatile salts) and target mitigation for poor populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reporting voyages, commodities, and ethnographic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The second volume of these voyages treats of East-India, and the neighbouring islands ... The author ... gives an exact list of all the merchantable commodities ... To all which he has annexed an account of the cheats used in divers of these commodities, especially in the silks, cloths, cottons, indigo. ... Among the many observables contained in this volume we take notice, that there are to be met with, admirable jugglers and mountebanks ... by some of whom the author affirms he saw done what follows: they kindled a great fire, and in it heated some iron chains red hot, which they laid about their bodies, without receiving any apparent hurt. ... He gives many particulars of divers kingdoms of the East.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting voyages and ethnographic observations, list commodities and known local adulterations/cheats, provide detailed first-hand descriptions of remarkable practices (including steps witnessed), and note sources and plausibility. Include trade routes, local production notes, and where possible, corroborating evidence for extraordinary claims.
